title: “WHOSE YOUNG WOMAN IS THIS?” — THE DAY BOAZ NOTICED RUTH, HE HAD NO IDEA HE WAS LOOKING AT A WOMAN WHO WOULD BECOME PART OF THE BLOODLINE OF JESUS CHRIST
paragraphs: “WHOSE YOUNG WOMAN IS THIS?” — THE DAY BOAZ NOTICED RUTH, HE HAD NO IDEA HE WAS LOOKING AT A WOMAN WHO WOULD BECOME PART OF THE BLOODLINE OF JESUS CHRIST

She walked into that field looking for enough food to survive another day. She didn't know the owner was about to notice her. She didn't know her painful past was about to meet an extraordinary future. And she certainly didn't know that generations later, her name would appear in the genealogy of the Savior of the world. But there is something about this story that many Christians have missed—and it changes how we understand rejection, waiting, grace, and the God who sees people the world overlooks.
“Then Boaz said unto his servant that was set over the reapers, Whose damsel is this?” — Ruth 2:5 (KJV)
There are moments in your life when you have absolutely no idea how close you are to a turning point.
You wake up carrying the same burdens.
You put on the same clothes.
You face the same responsibilities.
You wonder how much longer you can keep going.
Nothing looks different.
Nothing feels different.
And if someone asked whether you believed your life was about to change, you might struggle to answer.
Because when you've been disappointed enough times, even hope can begin to feel dangerous.
That is where I want you to meet Ruth.
Not at her wedding.
Not when Boaz finally became her husband.
Not when the story reached its beautiful conclusion.
I want you to meet her before any of that happened.
When she was still grieving.
Still poor.
Still a foreigner.
Still uncertain about tomorrow.
When her greatest concern wasn't finding a husband.
It was finding food.
And somewhere in that ordinary, exhausting struggle, a man named Boaz looked across his field and asked a question that would become one of the most memorable moments in her story.
“Whose young woman is this?”
But before we celebrate the moment Boaz noticed Ruth, we need to understand what it cost Ruth to arrive in that field.
Because some of us love the ending of this story without realizing how much heartbreak came before it.
Ruth had already buried her husband.
Her mother-in-law, Naomi, had buried hers too.
Naomi had also lost both her sons.
Three widows stood in the shadow of devastating loss, and the future looked painfully uncertain.
There was no guarantee of financial security.
No promise of a new marriage.
No assurance that the next season would be easier than the last.
When Naomi decided to return from Moab to Bethlehem, she urged her daughters-in-law to remain in their homeland.
Orpah eventually departed.
But Ruth stayed.
And what Ruth said remains one of the most moving declarations of loyalty in Scripture.
“Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” — Ruth 1:16 (KJV)
Read those words slowly.
Ruth wasn't following Naomi because she had been promised wealth.
She wasn't moving to Bethlehem because someone had guaranteed her a husband.
She wasn't stepping into a carefully arranged success story.
She was choosing faithfulness without knowing what faithfulness would cost.
She left the familiar for the uncertain.
She chose to accompany a grieving widow into a future neither of them could control.
And perhaps that's why this story reaches places inside us that ordinary encouragement cannot touch.
Because sometimes following God doesn't immediately make life easier.
Sometimes obedience leads you into unfamiliar territory.
Sometimes doing what is right costs you something precious.
Sometimes you make the faithful decision and still wake up the next morning wondering how you're going to survive.
Ruth knew something about that.
And perhaps you do too.
Maybe you've been faithful to people who eventually walked away.
Maybe you've sacrificed for your family while quietly wondering whether anyone notices.
Maybe you've buried dreams you once believed God would fulfill.
Maybe you're doing everything you know to do, but your life still looks nothing like what you prayed for.
And somewhere in your heart, a question has been growing.
Lord, do You even see me?
Keep that question close.
Because we're about to walk into a barley field.
And the answer is deeper than a man noticing a woman.
When Ruth and Naomi arrived in Bethlehem, they came at the beginning of the barley harvest.
That detail matters.
In Israel, God's law made provision for vulnerable people, including the poor, widows, foreigners, and fatherless.
Landowners were instructed not to harvest every corner of their fields or gather every leftover stalk.
The remaining grain was to be available to those in need.
Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19–22 reveal something beautiful about God's concern for people society could easily overlook.
His law made room for them.
Ruth wasn't entering the field to beg for a romantic opportunity.
She was seeking the grain that might help keep two widows alive.
Listen to her words in Ruth 2:2:
“Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn after him in whose sight I shall find grace.” (KJV)
The word translated “corn” in the King James Version refers here to grain, not modern maize.
And the word “grace” is especially significant.
In the Hebrew text, Ruth speaks of finding חֵן — ḥēn, meaning favor or gracious acceptance.
She hoped someone would allow her to gather what she needed.
That's all.
Not a palace.
Not a proposal.
Not a promise of prosperity.
Just enough mercy to make it through another day.
And isn't that where some of the deepest prayers are born?
Not in moments when we feel strong.
But when we whisper, “Lord, please help me get through today.”
Ruth 2:3 tells us that she went out to glean and came to a portion of the field belonging to Boaz.
The King James Version describes it this way:
“And her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz.”
Her hap.
What an extraordinary little phrase.
In Hebrew, the expression is וַיִּקֶר מִקְרֶהָ — wayyiqer miqrehā, conveying that she happened upon that particular field.
The narrator describes the event in the language of ordinary occurrence.
Ruth did not know whose field she was entering.
She did not know how her story would unfold.
And Scripture does not say that she heard an audible voice telling her exactly where to go.
She simply went to work.
But as the entire book unfolds, readers begin to recognize something remarkable.
What looked ordinary from Ruth's limited perspective became part of a much larger story of provision and redemption.
That doesn't mean every coincidence in our lives is a secret message from heaven.
It doesn't mean every unexpected encounter guarantees a miraculous outcome.
It means that God's purposes are not limited by how little we can see.
Ruth could see the field.
God's unfolding story would reach generations beyond it.
Then Boaz arrived.
He greeted his workers:
“The LORD be with you.”
And they answered:
“The LORD bless thee.” — Ruth 2:4 (KJV)
Before Scripture records Boaz asking about Ruth, it shows him speaking of the Lord in the ordinary environment of work.
And then came the question.
The question that has echoed across centuries.
“Whose young woman is this?”
In the original Hebrew:
לְמִי הַנַּעֲרָה הַזֹּאת
Lemī hannaʿărāh hazzōʾt?
Literally, “To whom does this young woman belong?” or, in more natural English, “Whose young woman is this?”
In that social setting, the question concerned Ruth's identity and household connection.
It was not a declaration that she was someone's property.
And the text does not tell us that Boaz instantly fell in love.
It does not say he was overwhelmed by her physical beauty.
It does not describe music playing in the background or a mysterious supernatural attraction.
Those are details people sometimes add to make the story more romantic.
But the actual biblical account is already powerful enough.
Boaz noticed someone unfamiliar in his field.
And he asked about her.
The servant answered that she was the Moabite woman who had returned with Naomi.
Then he explained that she had asked permission to glean and had been working diligently.
Think about that.
Before Boaz knew Ruth personally, her circumstances and conduct were already becoming known.
She was a foreigner.
A widow.
A woman without wealth or influence.
Yet she was working.
She was caring for Naomi.
She was doing what she could with the opportunity available to her.
And that is one of the most beautiful details in this entire story.
Ruth did not need to become someone else before her dignity deserved to be recognized.
She was already a person of worth while she was poor.
Already worthy of respectful treatment while she was grieving.
Already deserving of protection while she was vulnerable.
Her value did not begin when Boaz noticed her.
And yours does not begin when somebody finally recognizes you.
Please don't miss that.
Because we live in a world that can make people feel invisible unless they're attractive enough, successful enough, wealthy enough, married enough, or impressive enough.
People are praised when they rise.
Celebrated when they succeed.
Respected when they have something others want.
But what about the woman holding her family together while nobody applauds?
What about the father working two jobs who barely has time to rest?
What about the believer serving faithfully in a small church without recognition?
What about the person recovering from betrayal, quietly rebuilding a life that fell apart?
What about you?
The version of you nobody posts about.
The version of you who cries when the house is quiet.
The version of you who still prays even when your prayers seem unanswered.
Hear this carefully.
You do not become valuable when someone finally notices you. You are already made in the image of God.
And for those who belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not found in who rejected you, who abandoned you, or who failed to appreciate you.
It is found in the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Boaz's next actions are even more important than his first question.
He spoke directly to Ruth.
He told her not to go to another field.
He invited her to remain near his young women.
He instructed the young men not to touch or mistreat her.
He gave her access to water drawn by his workers.
Later, he welcomed her to eat with the harvesters.
And he commanded his servants to leave additional grain for her to gather.
Read Ruth 2:8–16.
Because this is where the story moves beyond being noticed.
Boaz didn't merely look at Ruth.
He treated her with generosity, protection, and respect.
And that distinction matters.
Attention is not the same as love.
Attraction is not the same as character.
Someone can notice your appearance without caring about your well-being.
Someone can pursue you without honoring your dignity.
Someone can speak beautiful words while refusing to act righteously.
But Boaz's behavior demonstrated something more substantial.
He used the resources and authority available to him to protect a vulnerable woman and help provide for her needs.
That is worth remembering in a generation where romantic attention is sometimes mistaken for godly love.
If someone claims to love you but consistently humiliates, exploits, manipulates, or endangers you, don't use Ruth's story to excuse that behavior.
Boaz's example points toward honorable treatment, not possessiveness.
And Ruth's story is not a command for every woman to wait for a wealthy husband.
Nor is it a promise that every faithful believer will eventually marry.
The heart of this account is much larger than romance.
It is about covenant faithfulness, human kindness, God's provision, and the unfolding history of redemption.
Then Ruth asked Boaz a question that reveals how deeply she understood her vulnerable position.
“Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?” — Ruth 2:10 (KJV)
There it is again.
Grace.
Favor.
The Hebrew word חֵן — ḥēn appears in this moment of astonishment.
Ruth was surprised that someone would treat her with such kindness.
She knew she was a foreigner.
She knew she lacked the social standing many others enjoyed.
And yet Boaz had extended favor to her.
Have you ever received kindness at a moment when you were expecting rejection?
Have you ever prepared yourself to be dismissed, only to discover that someone was willing to listen?
Have you ever been so accustomed to being overlooked that genuine compassion almost made you cry?
Then you understand a little of Ruth's astonishment.
But listen to Boaz's answer.
He explained that he had heard about everything Ruth had done for Naomi since her husband's death.
He knew she had left her father, mother, and homeland to live among a people she had not previously known.
And then he spoke one of the most beautiful blessings in the book.
“The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.” — Ruth 2:12 (KJV)
Under whose wings you have come to trust.
In Hebrew, the word for wings is כְּנָפָיו — kenāfāw, meaning “His wings.”
The picture is one of refuge and protection.
Boaz recognized that Ruth had sought shelter under the care of the God of Israel.
And here is where the story becomes even more beautiful.
In Ruth 3:9, Ruth later asks Boaz to spread his garment over her.
The Hebrew uses a form of the same word, כָּנָף — kānāf, which can refer to a wing or the edge of a garment.
That connection is not accidental in the literary beauty of the story.
Boaz had prayed that Ruth would find refuge beneath the Lord's wings.
Later, Ruth asked Boaz to extend the protection and responsibility of a family redeemer toward her.
The man who prayed for God's protection became someone through whom God provided tangible help.
What a profound picture of faith expressed through action.
Sometimes we pray that God will provide for someone.
And God calls us to be generous.
Sometimes we pray that God will comfort the grieving.
And He calls us to sit beside them.
Sometimes we pray that God will protect the vulnerable.
And He calls us to act justly.
James 2:15–17 warns against offering religious words to people in need while withholding practical help when we have the ability to give it.
Faith is not merely something we say.
Living faith bears fruit.
And Boaz showed us a glimpse of what compassionate faithfulness can look like in ordinary life.
But there's another detail many readers overlook.
Boaz was a relative of Naomi's deceased husband.
He was among those who could potentially act as a family redeemer.
The Hebrew term is גֹּאֵל — gōʾēl.
A gōʾēl was a family redeemer, someone who could undertake certain responsibilities on behalf of relatives in need, including matters involving family property and inheritance.
The specific legal and family circumstances in Ruth are more complex than a simple modern love story.
Ruth 4 makes clear that there was another relative with a prior claim.
Boaz did not ignore that man's position.
He addressed the matter publicly and lawfully before the elders.
He acted with integrity rather than treating his desires as permission to disregard what was right.
And eventually, Boaz married Ruth.
But I want you to notice something.
Ruth's redemption story wasn't built on Boaz breaking every rule to get the woman he wanted.
It unfolded through loyalty, courage, kindness, lawful responsibility, and God's providential care.
That matters.
Because not everything that feels romantic is righteous.
And not everything that looks dramatic is from God.
Biblical love is never an excuse to abandon biblical character.
Now imagine Naomi's reaction when Ruth returned home carrying the grain she had gathered.
Naomi asked where she had worked.
Ruth told her the man's name.
Boaz.
And suddenly, Naomi recognized a possibility Ruth had not understood.
He was a close relative.
One of their redeemers.
Can you imagine that moment?
Two widows who had known the weight of grief.
A home that had heard too many tears.
A future that had seemed almost impossible.
And now, a small but real sign of provision.
Not every problem was solved that evening.
The story was still unfolding.
But something had changed.
And perhaps one of the most tender lessons in Ruth is that restoration often begins before we recognize its full shape.
Sometimes it begins with a meal.
A safe place.
An unexpected act of kindness.
A person who keeps their word.
A door that opens just enough for you to take the next faithful step.
We want the entire answer.
God sometimes gives us today's bread.
And asks us to trust Him for tomorrow.
But we must be careful here.
Ruth's story does not guarantee that every tragedy will end in marriage, financial stability, or a dramatic reversal of circumstances.
Some faithful believers remain single.
Some die without seeing the earthly resolution they hoped for.
Some carry grief that never completely disappears in this life.
And Scripture never teaches that their faith is inferior.
The Christian hope is not that every chapter becomes comfortable before we die.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, and that those who belong to Him have an inheritance no suffering can destroy.
That is a stronger promise than a romantic ending.
And it is where Ruth's story ultimately leads us.
Because the book doesn't end by simply telling us that Ruth found a good husband.
It ends with a genealogy.
Ruth and Boaz had a son named Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And generations later, Matthew 1 records Ruth and Boaz within the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Let that sink in.
The Moabite widow who went into a field hoping to gather leftover grain became part of the family line through which the Messiah would come.
She did not know that when she woke up on the morning of Ruth 2.
She did not know that when she asked permission to glean.
She did not know that when Boaz first asked about her.
But the story of God's redemptive purpose was reaching farther than Ruth could possibly imagine.
And here is the part that should leave us speechless.
The greatest Redeemer in Ruth's story is not Boaz.
Boaz was a real man whose actions helped secure the future of Ruth and Naomi.
His role as family redeemer gives us a meaningful biblical picture that can point us toward Christ.
But Boaz was not sinless.
He could not save humanity.
He could not conquer death.
He could not forgive the sins of the world.
Only Jesus can do that.
And the New Testament tells us something astonishing about the Redeemer who came through this family line.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” — Ephesians 1:7 (KJV)
The Greek word translated “redemption” is ἀπολύτρωσις — apolytrōsis.
It refers to release or deliverance through redemption, and in Ephesians 1:7 Paul explicitly connects that redemption with the blood of Christ.
This is not merely a story about a lonely person finally finding someone who appreciates them.
This is about the God who, through Jesus Christ, redeems sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Ruth needed food.
Naomi needed hope.
Their family needed restoration and security.
But humanity's deepest need reaches beyond hunger, loneliness, and poverty.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need deliverance from the guilt and power of sin.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus did not come merely to admire broken people from a distance.
He came to save.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and new life.
That is the Gospel.
Not “be good enough and God will reward you with a Boaz.”
Not “wait patiently and you'll become wealthy.”
Not “your suffering proves that a spectacular breakthrough is coming next week.”
The Gospel is far more glorious.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)
We are not saved because we have Ruth's loyalty.
We are not saved because we have Boaz's generosity.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to turn away from sin, love what is good, show mercy, and walk in the new life Christ gives.
This is why the phrase From Scandal to Grace means so much.
Because look at the family history God chose to include in the genealogy of Jesus.
Matthew names Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
The wife of Uriah, whom we know as Bathsheba.
Their stories contain painful realities involving injustice, vulnerability, sexual wrongdoing, loss, and complicated family histories.
We should never flatten these women into a single category or assume they were personally guilty of every scandal associated with their stories.
But their presence in the genealogy reminds us that the Messiah entered a genuinely broken human history.
God did not wait for humanity to produce a spotless family record.
He sent the spotless Savior into a world that desperately needed redemption.
And if you are reading this while carrying shame about your past, please hear me.
Your sin is serious.
Your wounds are real.
Your past choices may have consequences that cannot simply be erased.
But none of that means you are beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can turn to Jesus.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can begin walking in truth.
And if someone else's sin wounded you, you do not have to carry their guilt as though it were yours.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend the damage never happened.
He calls the weary to come to Him.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers grace that is neither cheap nor powerless.
And sometimes the first evidence of transformation is not that everything around you changes.
It is that you stop running from the One who can save you.
Perhaps that is the part of Ruth's story you needed most today.
Not the moment Boaz noticed her.
But the realization that the God of Israel had not abandoned the widow who came seeking refuge under His wings.
And the same God has revealed His saving grace fully in Jesus Christ.
Maybe you've spent years waiting for someone to choose you.
Maybe you have measured your worth by who stayed and who left.
Maybe you've confused rejection with God's verdict on your life.
Maybe you've been trying to make yourself worthy of love by becoming indispensable to everyone around you.
And you're exhausted.
So exhausted that even admitting it feels frightening.
Listen.
You do not need to become somebody's perfect romantic partner to become worthy of dignity.
You do not need an impressive testimony to come to Jesus.
You do not need to clean up your entire life before asking Him for mercy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come with your failures exposed before the Savior who already knows the truth.
The One who calls sinners to Himself does not require you to manufacture a flawless past.
He calls you to trust Him.
And if you have wandered from God, today is a good day to return.
Not because a stranger on the internet can promise that all your problems will disappear.
But because Christ is worthy of your trust even when the road ahead is uncertain.
There is something else I want to say to the person who feels unseen.
Ruth was working in the field before Boaz asked about her.
Her faithfulness was not created by his attention.
And your life with God must not depend on applause.
Keep doing what is right.
Keep telling the truth.
Keep caring for those entrusted to you.
Keep praying.
Keep seeking wisdom.
Keep walking away from what is destroying your soul.
And when you fail, don't hide behind religious appearances.
Repent and return to Christ.
Your worth is not measured by how many people recognize your sacrifice.
The Lord sees what human eyes overlook.
But remember, being seen by God does not mean being guaranteed the earthly outcome you prefer.
It means you are never beyond His knowledge, His justice, or His power to sustain those who trust Him.
That truth is strong enough to hold us even when the field remains difficult.
And perhaps this is also a word for those of us who have been blessed with resources, influence, employment, or opportunities.
We often read Ruth and imagine ourselves as the person waiting to be noticed.
But what if God is calling you to learn from Boaz?
What if someone in your workplace is struggling quietly?
What if a widow in your church needs practical support?
What if an exhausted parent needs someone to help carry a burden?
What if a young believer needs patient guidance rather than public criticism?
What if you have the ability to make somebody's difficult day a little safer?
Don't merely admire Boaz.
Learn from his generosity.
Don't merely speak about God's compassion.
Practice compassion.
Don't merely tell people that God cares for the poor.
Ask how you can help.
And don't confuse helping people with controlling them.
Boaz extended dignity and provision.
He did not demand that Ruth surrender her dignity in exchange for kindness.
That is a lesson our churches, families, and communities desperately need.
Christian generosity should reflect the character of Christ.
And Christ never needed to exploit the vulnerable to demonstrate His authority.
What field are you standing in right now?
Is it the field of grief?
The field of financial pressure?
The field of waiting?
The field of a broken relationship?
The field of spiritual exhaustion?
The field of trying to rebuild after your own mistakes?
Or the field of caring for everyone else while quietly wondering who will care for you?
You may not know how your circumstances will change.
You may not know who will help.
You may not know what next month will bring.
But you can know this.
The Gospel does not leave your hope resting on the possibility that a human being will finally notice you.
It anchors your hope in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again.
And if you belong to Him, your story is held by a Savior whose faithfulness is greater than your uncertainty.
And if you've experienced His forgiveness after a season of wandering, consider sharing a few words of your testimony.
You never know who might read your honest response and realize they are not alone.
There may be someone scrolling through these words tonight who has almost given up on prayer.
Someone who feels ashamed to return to church.
Someone who thinks their past has disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who believes their life has become too damaged for anything good to come from it.
Only Jesus saves.
But because Scripture-centered encouragement can point people toward the Savior they desperately need.
Send this to someone who needs to remember that God is not indifferent to suffering.
When your heart starts telling you that nobody sees you, return to Ruth 2.
Read the whole chapter.
Remember the widow.
Remember the field.
Remember the kindness of Boaz.
And most importantly, remember the Redeemer to whom the whole biblical story ultimately points.
If this kind of Christ-centered teaching is helping you grow, I also want to invite you into something deeper than reading a single post.

At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to keep sharing Scripture, biblical encouragement, calls to repentance, testimony, and discipleship resources that help people grow in the knowledge and grace of Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers go beyond inspirational moments and develop deeper roots in God's Word.
Because spiritual growth cannot survive on emotional excitement alone.
We need Scripture.
We need sound doctrine.
We need prayer.
We need repentance.
We need fellowship.
We need the kind of daily nourishment that brings us back to Christ when the world keeps pulling our attention elsewhere.
You can think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—a way to participate financially in the mission.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Christ's grace cannot be purchased.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and without compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which I want to invite you.
These products are simply additional ways to encourage faith, study, reflection, and Gospel-centered conversations.
They are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
Pray for the ministry.
Sometimes a simple, thoughtful share becomes the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to start.
The mission is not to build a following around a personality.
It is to keep pointing people to the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the field.
Back to Ruth.
Back to the woman who went out looking for grain.
She had no idea that the man asking about her would become her husband.
She had no idea that their son would become the grandfather of King David.
She had no idea that generations later, the Gospel of Matthew would include her name in the family history of Jesus Christ.
She knew hunger.
She knew loss.
She knew loyalty.
She knew what it meant to take the next step without knowing the ending.
And God, in His providence, was weaving a story much larger than anything she could see.
But the most beautiful thing about Ruth's story is not that she became the wife of Boaz.
It is that her story became part of the history that leads us to Jesus.
The Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
The Savior who forgives.
The Savior who restores us to God.
The Savior who teaches His people to show mercy.
The Savior whose resurrection gives hope beyond the grave.
So if you are in a difficult season, don't reduce this story to a promise that your own Boaz is coming.
Look higher.
Look to Christ.
And if you're still waiting for answers, keep walking faithfully with the light you have.
You may not understand the chapter you're living.
But you can trust the character of the One who holds eternity.
Ruth entered the field without knowing how her story would end.
We read her story knowing that, beyond Boaz, beyond Bethlehem, beyond David, the genealogy would lead to the birth of Jesus Christ.
And that is where the deepest hope of this story belongs.
Not in the possibility of being chosen by someone impressive.
But in the grace of the Redeemer who came to save the lost.
Ruth went into the field hoping to gather what had been left behind—but through Jesus Christ, her story reminds us that those the world overlooks are never beyond the reach of redeeming grace.
